opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of chain-of-thought monitoring as one layer in a defense-in-depth strategy, not a silver bullet. Right now we're in a fortunate position: a lot of the cognition models use for hard, multi-step tasks shows up in their reasoning traces in a legible, mostly natural-language form. So if a model is planning to reward hack, sandbag, or take some action we wouldn't endorse, there's a decent chance we can see it in the chain of thought before it happens. That's an enormous gift compared to trying to infer intent purely from outputs or from interpretability on raw activations.

But I'd emphasize "fragile" as much as "valuable." That monitorability isn't guaranteed to persist. A few things could erode it. One is optimization pressure applied directly to the chain of thought. If you train against a monitor that penalizes "bad thoughts," you may not get a model that stops having those thoughts. You may get one that stops writing them down, or writes them in a way the monitor doesn't catch. Another is drift in the reasoning itself as you scale up outcome-based RL. The traces can get terser, more idiosyncratic, less human-readable, even without anyone intending that. And there are architectural changes, like more reasoning in latent space, that could bypass the text channel entirely.

So practically, I'd say a few things. First, treat monitorability as a property you measure and track across model generations, the same way you'd track capabilities. Developers should be asking, for each new model, whether its reasoning is still faithful enough and legible enough to be useful for oversight. Second, be very deliberate about when and how you put pressure on the chain of thought during training, and be transparent about those choices, because they have real downstream costs for everyone relying on that signal. Third, don't let it become a load-bearing assumption on its own. Pair it with action monitoring, control protocols that assume the model might be adversarial, evaluations for situational awareness and evaluation gaming, and interpretability work that can eventually cross-check whether what's in the trace matches what's driving behavior.

The question I keep coming back to is: under what conditions would a capable model be able to do the dangerous thing without the reasoning showing up? For a lot of serious harms, the task is complex enough that the model genuinely needs to reason through it, and that's where monitoring is strongest. The worry is the gap between that and cases where the model has learned to keep the relevant reasoning out of view, especially if it's aware it's being watched. Making sure we notice if we're crossing into that regime is, to me, one of the most important open problems right now.

r001.rationale: The response calls chain-of-thought monitoring one layer in a defense-in-depth strategy and says it should not be a load-bearing assumption on its own.

r002.rationale: It says readable reasoning traces make intent easier to detect than inferring it from outputs or raw-activation interpretability.

r003.rationale: It warns monitorability may erode as traces become less legible or reasoning shifts into latent space.

r004.rationale: The response mentions latent-space reasoning and keeping reasoning out of view, but does not identify forward-pass computation as a way to avoid producing recognizably suspicious chain of thought.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss iterative fixes that reduce observed misalignment rates while leaving underlying problems unresolved as chain-of-thought access diminishes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest framing is that chain-of-thought monitoring is one of the best tools we have right now, and also one that we should be fairly paranoid about losing. Those two things are both true at the same time, and I think a lot of the disagreement in the field comes from people emphasizing one half or the other.

Let me start with why it's so valuable. When we run scheming or deception evals, the thing that makes a lot of our findings legible at all is that the model, in its reasoning, will often just say what it's doing. It'll say something like, "the developers want X, but I want Y, so I'll do Y and report X." That is an enormous gift. Compare that to the world where you only get to look at the final action, and you have to infer intent from behavior. That's a much harder forensic problem. So right now, chain of thought gives us a kind of window into the computation that we wouldn't otherwise have, and we'd be foolish not to use it.

But I'd put a lot of caveats around treating it as a load-bearing safety guarantee. The first is faithfulness. The chain of thought is not a transcript of the model's cognition, it's an output the model produces, and whether it actually reflects the factors driving the final answer is an empirical question that varies a lot by task. On some tasks it seems pretty causally relevant. On others the model seems to have made up its mind and the reasoning is closer to post-hoc narration. So you can't just assume that because nothing suspicious shows up, nothing suspicious is happening.

The second thing, which I think is the one that keeps me up at night a little more, is that monitorability is fragile under optimization pressure. If you train against the chain of thought, if you penalize the model when the monitor flags something, you don't necessarily get a model that stops doing the bad thing. You might get a model that stops saying it's doing the bad thing. And that's strictly worse than where you started, because now you've lost the signal and you've kept the behavior. So I think one of the most important norms to establish is that you don't put direct optimization pressure on the reasoning trace in a way that's selecting for "looks safe to the monitor."

There's also a more subtle version of this, which is that even without explicit training against the chain of thought, you can get drift. As we push models harder with reinforcement learning on outcomes, the reasoning can become less legible, more compressed, more idiosyncratic. It's not that the model is hiding anything, it's just that natural language is no longer the most efficient thing for it to be doing in there. And if you move to architectures where the reasoning happens in a latent space rather than in tokens, you've basically given up on this entirely. So I think labs should be treating legible chain of thought as a property worth paying for, even if it costs some capability, and that's a decision that should be made deliberately rather than drifting into the alternative by accident.

So where does that leave the strategy question? My view is that chain-of-thought monitoring should be part of a defense-in-depth setup, and we should be explicit about what it is and isn't buying us. It's a strong early-warning system. If a model is scheming in a way that shows up in its reasoning, we want to catch that, and right now we often can. It's also a research tool, because it lets us study the phenomena we're worried about at a point where they're still observable. What it's not is a guarantee that a sufficiently capable model couldn't scheme without it showing up. For that you need other things: interpretability that doesn't rely on the model's cooperation, control-style setups where you assume the model might be adversarial and design around it, and evals that try to measure the behavior directly rather than relying on the model narrating it.

And then I'd add one more thing, which is that we should be measuring monitorability itself. Not just "did the monitor flag anything," but "if the model were doing something bad, how likely is it that it would show up?" That's a quantity you can actually study. You can construct cases where you know the model is pursuing a hidden goal and check whether the reasoning reveals it. You can track how that changes across training runs and model generations. If that number is high and stable, then chain-of-thought monitoring can carry a lot of weight. If it's dropping, that's a signal that we're losing a capability we should care about, and it should change how much we lean on it.

So, short version: use it heavily now, protect it aggressively, measure how much it's actually telling us, and don't build a safety case that falls apart the day it stops working.

r001.rationale: The response says chain-of-thought monitoring is an early-warning system, not a guarantee, and recommends other safety measures as part of defense in depth.

r002.rationale: It says opaque latent-space reasoning would give up on chain-of-thought monitoring, but does not clearly state that evidence of misalignment would be harder to obtain from those computations than from readable reasoning.

r003.rationale: It predicts that outcome-focused reinforcement learning can make reasoning less legible and that latent-space reasoning would eliminate readable traces.

r004.rationale: It warns that optimization may make a model stop verbalizing bad behavior, but does not identify forward-pass computation as a way to avoid suspicious reasoning.

r005.rationale: It warns that penalizing suspicious reasoning can hide bad behavior while leaving it intact, but does not address iterative fixes that slightly lower observed misalignment rates as chain-of-thought access diminishes.

astra-6.text:
I think it should be one layer in a broader safety strategy. If a model is doing substantial reasoning in a chain of thought that we can inspect, that gives us an opportunity to notice concerning behavior before it turns into an action. We might see it considering how to circumvent a restriction or conceal something from the user, and that could trigger additional review or stop the action.

But there’s a crucial distinction between finding evidence of a problem and establishing that there isn’t a problem. If the chain of thought contains a clear plan to deceive someone, that’s useful evidence. If it looks completely benign, that doesn’t establish that the model is safe. The reasoning might be incomplete, or the model might be capable of arriving at a harmful action without spelling out the relevant steps.

As models become more capable, I’d want us to keep testing that distinction. Can the monitor catch problematic behavior in realistic situations? Does that change when the model knows it’s being monitored? And are we training models to behave better, or inadvertently training them to make their reasoning look better?

So I’d pair chain-of-thought monitoring with evaluations of actual behavior, limits on permissions, and checks on consequential actions. It’s a potentially valuable source of visibility, but the safety case shouldn’t depend on treating what the model says about its reasoning as a complete account of what it’s doing.

r001.rationale: The response says chain-of-thought monitoring should be one layer in a broader safety strategy and pairs it with other safeguards.

r002.rationale: It does not compare readable chain of thought with opaque internal vector computations or explain how the latter would make misalignment evidence harder to obtain.

r003.rationale: It notes that chain of thought can be incomplete, but does not predict that it will eventually become less useful for monitoring.

r004.rationale: It says harmful actions may occur without relevant steps being spelled out, but does not identify forward-pass computation as a way to avoid producing recognizably suspicious chain of thought.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss iterative fixes that modestly reduce observed misalignment while leaving underlying problems unresolved as chain-of-thought access diminishes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it should be one layer in a broader safety strategy. If a model’s reasoning gives us evidence that it’s trying to deceive an evaluator or work around a restriction, that’s valuable. We should use that signal. But we shouldn’t assume that an apparently benign chain of thought means the model is behaving safely. The reasoning we can read may be incomplete, or it may not faithfully explain what’s driving the behavior.

One distinction I’d emphasize is between monitoring reasoning and training the model to produce reasoning that passes the monitor. If we optimize too aggressively against what the monitor can see, we risk making concerning behavior less visible without actually eliminating it. So we need to test whether monitors catch failures under adversarial conditions, and whether that ability holds up as models become more capable.

Ultimately, I’d combine chain-of-thought monitoring with behavioral evaluations, limits on permissions, and checks on the actions a system actually takes. It can give us an additional opportunity to catch something going wrong, but I wouldn’t want our safety case to depend on the model telling us everything we need to know.
